name: Warm-up Strategy
text:
# Warm-up Strategy

Also called: Encoder-freezing Warm-up, Warm-up

## Overview
A training phase that prevents the model from overfitting to the input view and ensures fine details are captured during distillation by temporarily freezing or adjusting objectives before full joint training [S1]. It builds on [Test-Time Finetuning](12983-test-time-finetuning.md) and serves as a stabilization mechanism for [radiance-field optimization](#44-radiance-field-optimization.md), particularly when introducing perceptual or adversarial losses that might otherwise cause mode collapse or weak distillation if applied immediately [S1, S2].

## How it works
**Inputs and Outputs:** Not given in the sources [G].
**Data Structures:** Not given in the sources [G].
**Steps:**
1. Initialize the scene representation and optimizer [G].
2. Determine the warm-up duration $T_{\text{warm}}$: 3,000 iterations for standard datasets (e.g., Deep Blending, [Mip-NeRF 360](#3306-mip-nerf-360.md), Tanks & Temples); 5,000 iterations for the BungeeNeRF dataset due to large-scale cityscape variations, inconsistent appearance, and geometry [S2].
3. Execute the warm-up phase for iterations $t < T_{\text{warm}}$:
   - Compute the base reconstruction loss $L_{\text{orig}}$ (e.g., standard 3DGS loss) [S2].
   - For the encoder-freezing variant (Pix2NeRF): Freeze the encoder parameters and update only the decoder/field parameters by minimizing $L_{\text{orig}}$ [S1].
   - For the WD Loss variant (3D [Gaussian Splatting](#946-gaussian-splatting.md)): Minimize only $L_{\text{orig}}$, excluding the perceptual WD loss [S2].
   - Update parameters using gradient descent on $L_{\text{total}} = L_{\text{orig}}$ [S1, S2].
4. Transition at iteration $t = T_{\text{warm}}$: Unfreeze the encoder if using the encoder-freezing variant [S1]. Enable the perceptual/WD loss component [S2].
5. Execute full training for iterations $t \ge T_{\text{warm}}$: Compute the total loss combining reconstruction and perceptual/adversarial objectives, then update parameters [S1, S2].

**Formulas:**
For the WD Loss variant, the total loss switches based on [iteration count](#1244-iteration-based-coloring.md):
$$ L_{\text{total}} = \begin{cases} L_{\text{orig}} & \text{if } t < T_{\text{warm}} \\ L_{\text{orig}} + \gamma L_{\text{wd}} & \text{if } t \ge T_{\text{warm}} \end{cases} $$
where $L_{\text{orig}}$ is the original rendering loss, $L_{\text{wd}}$ is the perceptual WD loss, and $\gamma$ is a dataset-calibrated scaling coefficient [S2]. During the warm-up phase of the encoder-freezing variant, the encoder parameters are fixed, so optimization minimizes only the reconstruction component relative to the frozen encoder output [S1].

**Parameters:**
- Warm-up iterations ($T_{\text{warm}}$): 3,000 for most datasets; 5,000 for BungeeNeRF [S2].
- Reconstruction weight ($\lambda_{\text{recon}}$): Must not be lowered to 1 in place of warm-up, as this breaks the balance between reconstruction and adversarial objectives [S1].

**Edge Cases and Pitfalls:**
- Mode collapse: Replacing warm-up with a lower reconstruction weight ($\lambda_{\text{recon}} = 1$) causes mode collapse for novel view synthesis because the balance between reconstruction and adversarial objectives is missing [S1].
- Weak distillation: If the encoder is never unfrozen after warm-up, the distillation remains relatively weak, resulting in few fine details [S1].
- Overfitting: Without warm-up, the model tends to overfit the input view and cannot produce meaningful content from novel poses [S1].
- Instability: For datasets with large-scale variations (e.g., BungeeNeRF), skipping warm-up or using insufficient iterations leads to instability caused by pruning and densification heuristics [S2].

## Subtopics

### Warm-up Strategy for WD Loss
A training initialization phase that uses the [original 3DGS loss](#15143-3d-gaussian-splatting-optimization.md) before introducing the perceptual WD objective to stabilize optimization, especially for datasets with large viewpoint/geometry variations [S2]. It is chosen when using WD-based losses (WD or [WD-R](#15613-wd-regularized-loss.md)) to prevent instability from pruning/densification heuristics and to provide a stable geometric initialization [S2]. It differs from the general encoder-freezing warm-up by focusing on loss landscape stability rather than encoder parameter constraints [S2].

## Operating characteristics
- Time Complexity: Adds $T_{\text{warm}}$ iterations of training to the total training time. For standard datasets, this is 3,000 iterations; for BungeeNeRF, 5,000 iterations [S2].
- Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources [G].
- Performance: Prevents overfitting to input views and mode collapse [S1]. Ensures fine details are captured during distillation [S1]. Provides a stable geometric initialization [S2].
- Strengths: Stabilizes optimization for perceptual losses; prevents mode collapse; improves novel view synthesis quality [S1, S2].
- Limitations: Increases total training time by the warm-up duration [S2]. Requires careful tuning of $T_{\text{warm}}$ for specific datasets (e.g., longer for BungeeNeRF) [S2].
- When to Use: When training radiance fields with perceptual/adversarial losses (e.g., Pix2NeRF, WD-3DGS) to avoid overfitting or instability [S1, S2].
- When Not to Use: Not given in the sources [G].

## Background
The warm-up strategy originated in the context of unsupervised single-shot novel view synthesis, specifically in the Pix2NeRF framework [S1]. It was introduced to address the tendency of GAN-based distillation methods to overfit to the input image or collapse into trivial solutions when adversarial and reconstruction losses are balanced improperly [S1]. Later, similar warm-up concepts were adopted in 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization to stabilize the introduction of perceptual losses (WD loss) in large-scale cityscape datasets [S2].
